_about: Plain-language pass over cpl_memory `title` and `plain` — the two READER-FACING fields, rendered by the Report view and (as of this run) sent to the model by the Briefing. Keyed by the row's write key: `slug`, or the uuid where slug is null. `summary` and `detail` were NOT touched — they are the precise curator record.
_method: Guarded UPDATE ... FROM (VALUES ...) matched on coalesce(slug, id::text), with a no-op guard (`m.title is distinct from s.t`). All 202 keys were verified to match exactly one live row BEFORE any write — a key that names nothing returns success and changes nothing (see the `a-write-key-can-name-nothing-and-look-like-auth` row).
_verified_after: 0 rows without plain text, 0 rows carrying developer jargon and 0 British spellings across all 573 non-superseded rows. 7 superseded rows were left alone — they render on no surface.

haiku-drops-a-say-this-whenever-caveat.title: On the smaller model, Sierra drops the caution that the credit backlog is a ceiling, not a debt
haiku-drops-a-say-this-whenever-caveat.plain: Sierra now runs on a smaller, cheaper AI model. Testing found one thing she stops saying: that the roughly one million units of credit waiting to be acted on is a ceiling rather than a debt, because about 30% of it will correctly turn out not to apply. The instruction telling her to say it is still there and is perfectly clear, so this is her not following it rather than us forgetting to ask. Everything else we test still passes.

sb135-created-ed-code-article-9-for-cpl.title: A new state law put credit for prior learning into the Education Code, and one register row now asks for something already enacted
sb135-created-ed-code-article-9-for-cpl.plain: A new state law, in force since 13 July 2026, wrote credit for prior learning into California's Education Code for the first time. It requires every campus to accept credit for prior learning that another campus has already transcribed, including toward general education, transfer and the major. Our regulation register still lists that as something to be won. It also gives several other rows a footing in law they did not have, and it works against one of them.

surface-vocabulary-is-five-places-not-th.title: Letting the assistant work on a new screen takes five separate edits, and no one document listed them all
surface-vocabulary-is-five-places-not-th.plain: When we let the assistant work on a new screen, five separate places have to be told about it. Our written notes listed three; a memory entry listed a different three. Both said three, and the real answer is the two lists put together, which is five. Miss one and the screen quietly gets the wrong size limit, or no curator can ever aim a rule at it, or it never shows up in the picker. Reading the memory table before starting is what caught this.

a-client-cannot-see-the-cap-the-server-e.title: A page cannot tell whether the service behind it has been updated yet, so the gap between them is silently wrong
a-client-cannot-see-the-cap-the-server-e.plain: The two halves of a feature go live at different moments: the page the moment work is merged, the service behind it only when someone deploys it. In the gap, the page sends a long request that the older service quietly trims to its first 1,000 characters - throwing away the instructions at the end - and the answer comes back as confident prose instead of the structured result we asked for. The page checks the size limit written in its own copy of the code, not the one actually deployed, and our automated tests check the deployed service, so neither can see the mismatch. The defense is to put the subject first, so anything cut off fails loudly instead of quietly.

gr-instrument-doctrine-is-measured-and-a.title: The rule for telling law from regulation from practice was measured from CPL's own rows, and must not be pointed at the sample area
gr-instrument-doctrine-is-measured-and-a.plain: We worked out how to tell whether a change needs new legislation, a change to regulation, or nothing more than a memo - and we checked the rule against our own CPL rows rather than just asserting it: three out of three one way, two out of two the other. But it is a generalization drawn from one subject area, so it is tied to that area by name rather than guessed from the wording. The dual-enrollment area is a deliberate sample whose rows are neutral review prompts, not positions we hold; running the CPL rule there would invent a Chancellor's Office position nobody took.

a-substring-match-cannot-fail-on-a-typo.title: A check that looks for a name inside a longer text cannot catch a typo in that name
a-substring-match-cannot-fail-on-a-typo.plain: A test confirmed a setting existed by looking for its name somewhere inside a block of text. That also matches the name with a typo stuck on the end, so the single most likely real mistake could not fail the test. We only found it by deliberately breaking each check one at a time and watching which ones stayed green while the others went red.

an-area-sweep-sees-what-a-per-row-pass-c.title: Sam: the whole-area sweep is the routine, and three of its findings cannot be seen one row at a time
an-area-sweep-sees-what-a-per-row-pass-c.plain: Sam asked for the review we ran by hand to become a button he can press after editing. It is not the single-row review made wider: three of the findings that mattered are invisible from inside any one row. The headline - that a row asks for something already enacted - only appears when the row is read against a document about the whole area. Whether a row was weakened is a comparison between rows. And a duty that no row covers at all is not a finding about any row.

a-rotating-token-in-a-shared-store-has-n.title: A stale browser tab overwrote the live sign-in with an expired copy and signed every tab out
a-rotating-token-in-a-shared-store-has-n.plain: Sign-ins renew themselves, and each renewal cancels the one before it. Our code let any open browser tab declare its own copy the true one - so a tab that had been sitting idle published its already-cancelled copy over the live one, and everything signed out. Sam hit this mid-edit on the regulation register with several tabs open, and the save failed with a message blaming his account, which was fine all along. The audit trail settled it: every save that worked left a record behind and his left none. The freshest copy wins now.

gr-sensitivity-open-rows-already-exist.title: Some regulation rows are already marked shareable - our own notes said none were
gr-sensitivity-open-rows-already-exist.plain: Our project notes said every row in the regulation register was marked internal-only, and that opening any of them was Sam's call. Checked against the live data, some are already open. This matters before anything is exported, because the caution about unverified legal text travels with the export. Measured the same day: not one of the twenty rows has been verified by anybody. For a document heading to the Chancellor's Office that is the number to move, and it is a person's job rather than something software can do.

a-write-key-can-name-nothing-and-look-li.title: A save aimed at a row that does not exist looks exactly like being signed out
a-write-key-can-name-nothing-and-look-li.plain: The Memory tab saved changes by naming the row with its short text handle. That handle is optional, and six of the 572 entries do not have one - so for those, the save was addressed to nothing, changed nothing, and reported no error at all. The page read that silence as a rejected sign-in and told Sam his team phrase had expired, which was untrue and sent him looking in the wrong place entirely. Saves now use the row's permanent identifier, and a row that cannot be named is refused out loud.

a-status-cycle-writes-what-it-passes-thr.title: A button that cycles through states saves every state it passes through
a-status-cycle-writes-what-it-passes-thr.plain: One button stepped an entry through three states in a loop. Getting from the first to the third meant passing through the middle one - and on a live table each step was a real save with a real audit record. Sam's two clicks are recorded fifteen seconds apart, and they left one entry marked out-of-date while also carrying a verification stamp for a check nobody ever performed. It is a menu now: one click, one save, and each choice says what it means.

a-crashing-test-leaves-later-checks-unre.title: A test that stops on a missing item never reports the checks below it
a-crashing-test-leaves-later-checks-unre.plain: Five times in one session a deliberate fault reported no failures - because the test had crashed partway through on something that was not there and stopped, so the checks after it never ran. The result only said that something failed, not what. Two rules follow: look for a missing item in a way that reports absence as an answer rather than crashing, and never let a run report success merely because it reached the end.

blast-rank-is-computed-by-nothing.title: The impact ranking on the regulation rows was typed in by hand - nothing calculates it
blast-rank-is-computed-by-nothing.plain: Sam asked for a re-analysis of the regulation priorities. Checking first showed there was nothing to re-run: the impact ranking on those rows was written by hand, and no part of the system produces it. All sixteen CPL rows carry one and the four sample rows carry none. Building the button would have meant inventing an analysis and calling it a re-run. We built the checks a lawyer makes first instead, which is an answer that can be defended to the Chancellor's Office.

cpl-sb-return-tab-was-per-browser-tab.title: The note saying which screen to return to after signing in was left where the new tab could not read it
cpl-sb-return-tab-was-per-browser-tab.plain: Signing in by emailed link opens a brand-new browser tab. Nine parts of the site left a note saying which screen to come back to, but they left it somewhere only the original tab can read. So everyone, signing in from anywhere, landed on the same default screen. The file that manages sign-ins even described that note as the thing that returns you to the right screen, while it could not. The note now lives where both tabs can see it, expires after half an hour so an overnight one cannot hijack an unrelated sign-in, and is used once.

sam-accepts-the-haiku-caveat-gap.plain: Sierra now runs on a smaller, cheaper AI model while our billing is sorted out. On that model she drops one caution: that the roughly one million units of credit waiting to be acted on is a ceiling, not a debt - about 30% of it will correctly turn out not to apply. Sam was shown this and said he can live with it for now, so nobody should go and fix it on their own initiative. The fix is written up and ready if he changes his mind.

sam-verified-sierra-on-haiku.plain: Sam read Sierra's answers in a browser after she was moved to the smaller, cheaper model and said they look good. We can prove the right version is running; only a person can say whether the answers actually read well, and that is what closes out a change to Sierra. The move is temporary, until corporate billing is released.
